title: AI Hallucination Cases Database — Global Tracker of AI-Generated False Citations in Legal Proceedings
author: Damien Charlotin

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: Charlotin’s database materially develops the cluster’s proposition by documenting varied judicial consequences and concrete failures of human verification, while expressly limiting its 1,174-case inventory so it is not mistaken for a prevalence or model-error measure.
qs: It does not track the (necessarily wider) universe of all fake citations or use of AI in court filings.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source materially strengthens the cluster’s verification-risk proposition by documenting a large, cross-jurisdictional set of legal-proceeding incidents involving fabricated material, false quotations and misrepresentation, including incidents involving lawyers and pro se litigants. It also extends the practical response by developing an automated reference checker, although it supplies no validation evidence for that tool and does not address productivity gains or lawyer replacement.
qs: Roscoe, "18 Lawyers Caught Using AI Explain Why They Did It (404 Media, 30 September 2025)  If you know of a case that should be included, feel free to contact me.3  (Readers may also be interested in this project regarding AI use in academic papers.)  Based on this database, I have developped an automated reference checker that also detects hallucinations: PelAIkan.

st.t: Litigation responsibility: Sanctions follow conduct and authority
st.an: The database accepts the cluster’s core account and materially extends its case-level evidence through additional reports of fabricated authorities, failures of verification and supervision, deficient correction, and varied remedies. Its strongest contribution is documenting both unequivocal human responsibility for filed AI content and the absence of any automatic sanction, with outcomes ranging from warnings to financial, procedural and professional penalties.
qs: An attorney who files a document containing AI-generated content is responsible for that content, fully and without qualification.
The court cautioned compliance with the Illinois Supreme Court Policy on AI but imposed no sanctions and affirmed the judgment due to an inadequate record on appeal.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The tracker materially strengthens the cluster’s verification and governance claims with cross-jurisdictional court-record evidence. It links serious failures to unverified or uncontrolled AI use, documents concrete professional and case consequences, and shows courts imposing verification-focused remedies, while also confirming that responses vary by context. It does not independently address the cluster’s broader productivity, capability-frontier or operating-model claims.
qs: The attorney filed the document without verifying its contents.

Court capped sanctions at $10,000, required a replacement brief limited to accurately described authorities, and required certification that no generative AI was used to draft the brief and that cited authorities were verified.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: AI use does not displace lawyers’ professional responsibility, and sanctions respond to failures of supervision, verification, candor and correction rather than to AI use itself. Its incident inventory also supports treating hallucination cases as documented court events, not general model-reliability measurements.
qs: The duty to verify, the duty of candor, the duty of competence, and the duty of supervision cannot be delegated to a machine.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: Charlotin’s tracker supports the cluster by documenting a large and growing body of judicial decisions involving reliance on hallucinated legal material. Its careful scope limits also reinforce the cluster’s distinction between realised court incidents and general model error rates: the database is provisional and does not measure all false citations or AI-assisted filings.
qs: Notably, this does not cover mere allegations of hallucinations, but only cases where the court or tribunal has explicitly found (or implied) that a party relied on hallucinated content or material.
While seeking to be exhaustive (**1174** cases identified so far), it is a work in progress and will expand as new examples emerge.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal framing of legal AI as a supervised aid: it accepts AI’s potential utility while holding that lawyers remain fully accountable for AI-assisted filings and cannot delegate verification, competence, candor or supervision. Its sanctions account also illustrates the consequences of unchecked use rather than opposing AI categorically.

kp.k: Database documents judicially addressed hallucinations, not overall AI usage
kp.d: Charlotin reports 1174 identified cases in a work-in-progress database, with coverage beginning Q2 2023 and the latest displayed decision dated 23 March 2026. Its unit is legal decisions addressing AI use beyond a passing reference. Inclusion generally requires a court or tribunal to find or imply reliance on hallucinated material, with discretionary exceptions for alleged but unconfirmed AI use. These are incident counts, not measured model error rates or a census of AI use in filings.
qs: While seeking to be exhaustive (**1174** cases identified so far), it is a work in progress and will expand as new examples emerge.
It does not track the (necessarily wider) universe of all fake citations or use of AI in court filings.
Notably, this does not cover mere allegations of hallucinations, but only cases where the court or tribunal has explicitly found (or implied) that a party relied on hallucinated content or material.
As an exception, the database also covers some judicial decisions where AI use was alleged but not confirmed. This is a judgment call on my part.
From period: Q2 2023

kp.k: Recorded incidents span jurisdictions and professional roles
kp.d: The displayed jurisdiction counts include USA 787, Canada 130, Australia 62, UK 50 and Israel 43, alongside numerous other jurisdictions and international arbitration. Party categories include 696 pro se litigants, 447 lawyers, 16 judges, 10 experts, four prosecutors, two paralegals, one arbitrator and one federal defender. The database therefore records incidents involving both represented and self-represented parties, as well as other participants in legal proceedings; these counts describe its coverage rather than comparative rates of misconduct.

kp.k: Court treats verification and supervision as nondelegable duties
kp.d: In the quoted State v. Coleman decision of 20 March 2026, the Ohio appellate court recognises AI's potential benefits but holds attorneys fully responsible for filed AI-generated content. The court explicitly preserves duties of verification, candor, competence and supervision under professional and court rules; this is the court's position reproduced by the database, not an independent empirical finding by its author.
qs: To the contrary, this court recognizes that AI is an inevitable and potentially beneficial feature of modern legal practice.
An attorney who files a document containing AI-generated content is responsible for that content, fully and without qualification.
The duty to verify, the duty of candor, the duty of competence, and the duty of supervision cannot be delegated to a machine.

kp.k: Delegated drafting produced fabricated evidence and compounded misconduct
kp.d: The Coleman court describes an attorney allowing non-attorney staff to prepare an appellate filing with a public generative AI platform. Fabricated transcript quotations were filed without verification, and the attorney subsequently failed to correct or disclose them. The court also describes an apparently AI-generated policy with unfilled placeholders and a later filing containing an embedded ChatGPT prompt. The database records a 2000 USD sanction, bar referral, disqualification, notification obligations, CLE and an apology letter.
qs: The AI tool fabricated transcript quotations—attributing specific, inflammatory statements to a real prosecutor that were never spoken.
The attorney filed the document without verifying its contents. When the fabrications were identified, he did not correct the record.
He proffered an AI policy that itself appeared to have been generated by AI, complete with unfilled placeholder brackets.
Two months after a sanctions hearing, a filing in another court bore the unmistakable hallmarks of unchecked AI output, including a ChatGPT prompt embedded in the text of a legal brief.
Monetary Sanction; Bar Referral; Counsel disqualified in this case; Order to notify the judgment in other cases; CLE; Letter of apology

kp.k: Judicial remedies include financial and case-dispositive consequences
kp.d: Displayed decisions record consequences beyond warnings. Couvrette v. Wisnovsky, dated 23 March 2026, lists struck briefs, a 15.5k monetary sanction, 94.7k adverse costs and dismissal with prejudice, with 109700 USD in the monetary field. Prososki v. Regan, dated 20 March 2026, records a struck appellate brief, dismissal of the appeal and bar referral. In Ben-Cohen v. Municipality of Ramat Gan, dated 22 March 2026, the database reports that Israel's Supreme Court accepted an appeal based on the municipality's reliance on nonexistent authorities attributed to uncontrolled AI use and ordered 30,000 ILS costs.
qs: Briefs struck; Monetary sanction (15.5k); Adverse costs order (94.7k); claims dismissed with prejudice
Appellant's brief stricken; appellant's appeal dismissed; Bar referral
The Supreme Court found these to be the product of uncontrolled AI use, accepted the appeal on that basis and ordered costs of 30,000 ILS against the municipality.

kp.k: Courts impose specific safeguards on replacement legal submissions
kp.d: The Doiban v. Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission entry, dated 18 March 2026, reports at least 15 fabricated case citations and at least nine nonexistent quotations. Counsel acknowledged unverified search-engine results and some AI use for an outline. The court capped sanctions at $10,000 and required a replacement brief containing accurately described authorities, certification of authority verification and certification that generative AI had not drafted the brief. Another displayed decision, In re Scott Mitchell Obeginski, affirmed an order requiring copies of cited authorities.
qs: Petitioner’s opening brief contained at least 15 fabricated case citations and at least nine purported quotations that do not exist in Oregon case law; counsel acknowledged reliance on unverified search-engine results and some use of AI for an outline.

kp.k: Recorded hallucination incidents do not uniformly result in sanctions
kp.d: The displayed outcomes include warnings, admonishments, permission to correct briefs and decisions not to sanction. In Kateryna Maslovska v. Ekaterina Shigabetdinova, dated 11 March 2026, the database reports six AI-style citations across both parties' briefs, but no sanctions; affirmance rested on an inadequate appellate record. In Checks Aciek Ateny Nai v. National Asset Mortgage, LLC, et al., the court declined Rule 11 sanctions after the show-cause order was satisfied. These examples distinguish recorded incidents from completed punitive outcomes.
qs: Appellate court found briefs from the parties contained six AI-style citations (four from defendant, two from plaintiff) that either did not exist or did not support the propositions for which they were cited.
The court cautioned compliance with the Illinois Supreme Court Policy on AI but imposed no sanctions and affirmed the judgment due to an inadequate record on appeal.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Charlotin documents generative-AI hallucinations entering legal proceedings and records resulting procedural, financial and professional consequences.
pts.d: The source's principal contribution is descriptive rather than predictive: AI-generated material in proceedings includes fabricated authorities, false quotations and other erroneous arguments or submissions. Charlotin's case summaries associate these incidents with warnings, struck briefs, monetary sanctions, adverse costs orders, disciplinary referrals and, in some cases, dismissal. Outcomes vary; some entries record no sanctions. The quoted State v. Coleman court, rather than Charlotin himself, states that AI may benefit practice but cannot displace attorneys' verification and professional duties. That judicial statement should not be treated as Charlotin's own prediction. Separately, Charlotin claims to have developed PelAIkan, an automated reference checker that detects hallucinations; the excerpt supplies no quantified performance results.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of a curated database of 1,174 identified cases and individual judicial decisions, not a model benchmark or a measured hallucination rate.
pts.d: Charlotin reports jurisdiction, participant, tool attribution, error type and outcome for judicially addressed incidents. The snapshot lists 978 entries under Fabricated, 309 under False Quotes, 478 under Misrepresented and 27 under Outdated Advice; these categories overlap and should not be added as mutually exclusive cases. Illustrative summaries include Doiban, where the source reports at least 15 fabricated citations, at least nine nonexistent quotations and a $10,000 sanction, and Ben-Cohen, where it reports an appeal accepted on the basis of uncontrolled AI use and costs of 30,000 ILS against a municipality. Some AI attribution is implied or unidentified rather than established through a named tool. The database supplies evidence of documented incidents and responses, but provides no denominator for all AI-assisted filings and no comparative tool-performance evaluation. PelAIkan's detection claim is supported by an invitation to examine reports or request a demo, rather than reported accuracy data.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The snapshot covers incidents from Q2 2023 through displayed decisions dated March 2026, subject to explicit inclusion and attribution qualifications.
pts.d: The latest displayed decision is dated 23 March 2026. The total is a work-in-progress count rather than a forecast or a demonstrated trend in incidence. Inclusion generally requires a court or tribunal to address AI use substantively and explicitly find or imply reliance on hallucinated material. Charlotin allows discretionary exceptions where AI use was alleged but not confirmed. The database expressly excludes the wider universe of fake citations and AI use in court filings. Its recorded consequences concern particular proceedings and conduct, especially reliance on unverified content; they are not presented as inevitable consequences of every use of legal AI. No adoption, employment or market-transformation forecast is supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Recorded incidents affect represented and self-represented litigants, lawyers and other participants across multiple jurisdictions, with consequences for both professional accountability and litigation outcomes.
pts.d: The participant filters list 696 pro se litigant entries and 447 lawyer entries, alongside judges, experts, prosecutors, paralegals, an arbitrator and a federal defender. These are database classifications, not population-level incidence rates or necessarily mutually exclusive groups. Jurisdiction counts are concentrated in the USA (787), with Canada (130), Australia (62), the UK (50), Israel (43) and other jurisdictions also represented. Lawyers face sanctions, referrals, disqualification and corrective requirements; litigants can face struck submissions, dismissal or adverse costs. Municipal clients are also affected, as illustrated by Ben-Cohen. The Doiban summary records added verification and replacement-brief requirements. The source does not segment effects by law-firm size, staffing structure, billing model or legal-service market share.
